n: Balance is the state of equilibrium between parts of a design, achieved through the distribution of "visual weight" across an axis or center point. Unity is the near miss: it concerns whether the parts belong together, not whether they are in equilibrium.

q: Water features, rustling plants, and birds are cited as sources of which landscape element?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Sound
n: Sound, produced by water features, rustling plants, or birds, can enhance the ambiance of a landscape. Its inclusion is the point worth noting — landscape design addresses more than the visual senses.

q: Softscape refers to which components of a landscape?
o: All the living components — plants, soil, turf, and other organic materials
The temporary furnishings and movable planters
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Softscape
n: Softscape is all the living components of a landscape — the plants, soil, turf, and other organic materials. The non-living, solid, man-made elements are hardscape, which forms the framework softscape is arranged within.

q: Within architecture, design principles are:
o: The fundamental conceptual tools used to organize and arrange architectural elements into a cohesive and meaningful whole
The material specifications recorded in a project manual
The stylistic labels used to date a building
The statutory minimums that govern building dimensions
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles
n: Design principles are conceptual tools for organizing and arranging elements into a cohesive, meaningful whole — they govern relationships, not measurements. Statutory minimums are code requirements, which constrain a design without organizing it.

q: Which landscape element covers the layout and the open or closed feeling of an area, as well as how areas are connected?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Space
n: Space is the layout and the open or closed feeling of the area, and it also covers how the areas connect to one another. Line contributes to that by defining edges, but connection and enclosure are the business of space.

q: Which set of problems is listed as a challenge of softscape rather than hardscape?
o: Becoming too dominant or sterile in a composition
Water pooling and inadequate surface drainage
High installation cost and difficulty of modification
Consistent care, vulnerability to climate and pests, and seasonal replacement
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Softscape — Challenges
n: Softscape requires consistent care such as watering, pruning, and fertilizing, may be affected by climate, pests, or diseases, and needs seasonal planning and replacement. High installation cost, drainage failure, and sterility are the challenges the module attaches to hardscape.

q: Articulating the importance or significance of a form or space by its size, shape, or placement relative to the other forms and spaces of the organization defines which principle?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles — Hierarchy (Ching, F. D. K., 2014; Unwin, S., 2013, Analysing Architecture)
n: Hierarchy is the articulation of a form's or space's importance by its size, shape, or placement relative to the rest of the organization — it is a comparative ranking within a whole. Emphasis is the close relative: it makes one element stand out, but hierarchy orders the entire set.

q: How do hardscape elements behave over time?
o: They decompose and enrich the surrounding soil
They are seasonal and need replacing each year
They grow and spread if not maintained
They are fixed and permanent, usually requiring construction and remaining static
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Hardscape — Key Features, Fixed and permanent
n: Hardscape elements are fixed and permanent: they usually require construction and remain static over time. Softscape is the opposite case — dynamic, changing with the seasons, and needing active maintenance.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: How are palms most effectively planted for better visual impact and a slight increase in shade?
o: As single isolated stalks at wide intervals
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Palm Trees, Effectiveness in Sun shading
n: Palms are often more effective in shade, and give better visual impact, when planted in "naturalistic" clusters rather than as single isolated stalks. Grouping is what compensates for the thinness of any one crown.

q: A colonnade guides the eye along a hall through the patterned recurrence of its columns. Which principle does this describe, and by which three devices is it produced?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles — Rhythm (Ching, F. D. K., 2014, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order)
n: Rhythm is movement characterized by the patterned recurrence of architectural elements, guiding the eye through a space by repetition, alternation, or progression. Hierarchy is the near miss because it also uses size and placement, but its purpose is to rank importance rather than to create movement.

q: Which driveway surface is described as decorative with old-world charm, though less smooth?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Driveways and Parking Areas, Examples
n: Cobblestone drives are decorative and carry old-world charm, at the cost of a less smooth surface. Exposed aggregate concrete is the other textured option, but it is valued specifically for being slip-resistant.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Under "How Trees Provide Effective Sun Shading," which three species are named as excellent in tropical climates for canopy density?
o: Jacaranda, Fire Tree, and Palawan Cherry
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: How Trees Provide Effective Sun Shading — Canopy Density
n: Thicker foliage means better shade, and Narra, Acacia, and Mango are named excellent for tropical climates on that measure. Pine and Spruce are dense too, but the module lists them under pyramidal/conical shapes suited to windbreaks rather than tropical shade.

q: In the Classical tradition, which dimension serves as the "Module," the basic unit from which the rest of an order is proportioned?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Theories of Proportion — The Classical Orders
n: In the Classical Orders the diameter of the column serves as the Module, so every other dimension is expressed as a multiple or fraction of it. The entablature height is a derived figure, not the base unit.

q: Which decorative element offers rest spots and blends seamlessly with planters or retaining walls?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Structural and Decorative Elements, Examples
n: Benches and seating walls offer rest spots and blend seamlessly with planters or retaining walls — the same detail noted earlier when retaining walls are said to double as informal seating. Pergolas serve shade and vertical framing instead.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Fruit-bearing trees are called the staples of which kind of landscape, and what do they do to a site?
o: "Edible Landscapes"; they turn it from a passive space into a productive one
"Healing gardens"; they turn it into a therapeutic space
"Dry landscapes"; they turn it into a contemplative space
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Fruit-bearing Trees
n: Fruit-bearing trees are the staples of "Edible Landscapes" and turn a site from a passive space into a productive one, providing both fruit and shade. Dry landscape is a different idea entirely — the Japanese Zen garden discussed later in this module.

q: The Ken, the Japanese vernacular modular system, evolved from which two references?
o: The length of a roof beam and the pitch of a rafter
The height of a doorway and the reach of an arm
The width of a shoji screen and the depth of an engawa
The size of a floor mat (Tatami) and the distance between columns
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Theories of Proportion — The Ken
n: The Ken evolved from the size of the Tatami floor mat and the distance between columns, giving a flexible grid that allows both standardized construction and varied spatial experiences. It is a vernacular system, developed by building practice rather than derived from a theorist's ratio.

q: Which patio surface is described as durable and elegant and suited for Mediterranean or modern styles?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Decks and Patios, Examples
n: Stone or tile patios are durable and elegant and suit Mediterranean or modern styles. Stamped concrete is the budget stand-in for the same look, which is why it is the option most easily confused with it.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: The caution the reviewer raises about an ornamental tree's appearance across the year is:
o: It may look stunning for about two weeks of flowering but "skeletal" or sparse the rest of the year
It grows too fast and requires annual replacement
Its flowers stain paving beneath it
It changes colour unpredictably with soil chemistry
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Ornamental/Flowering Trees
n: An ornamental that looks stunning for two weeks of flowering might read as "skeletal" or sparse for the remaining fifty. That is a design risk when the tree is carrying a focal point that must work all year.

q: Placing different elements side by side to intensify their individual characteristics — through changes in colour, texture, shape, or material — is which principle?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Contrast
n: Contrast is the juxtaposition of different elements to intensify their individual characteristics, achieved through changes in colour, texture, shape, or material. Unity works in the opposite direction, tying elements together rather than sharpening their differences.

q: Fences and screens define boundaries, ensure privacy, and block unwanted views or wind. What further benefit can they give when lined with dense vegetation or sound-absorbing panels?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, pp. 62–63: Hardscape — Fences and Screens
n: Fences can also reduce noise pollution when lined with dense vegetation or sound-absorbing panels. The fence alone is a visual and wind barrier; it is the added mass and softness that handles sound.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which physical trait makes most palms ideal for tight urban spaces or planting near foundations and sidewalks?
o: Their ability to be pruned to any height
Their relatively small, non-invasive root balls and narrow trunks
Their tolerance of shade from adjacent buildings
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Palm Trees
n: Most palms have relatively small, non-invasive root balls and narrow trunks, so they can sit close to foundations and sidewalks without lifting them. Fruit trees are the direct contrast — their aggressive, thirsty roots can crack the same surfaces.

q: Which later housing ideas does Unité d'Habitation influence, according to the reviewer?
o: Heritage conservation districts and adaptive reuse
Pocket parks, micro-retreats, and vacant-lot infill
Urban housing blocks, co-living spaces, and green roofs
Suburban subdivisions, cul-de-sacs, and gated villages
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Unité d'Habitation, Modern Influence
n: Its modern influence is on urban housing blocks, co-living spaces, and green roofs — each a direct descendant of the modular unit, the communal space, and the roof garden. Pocket parks come from the parks section of this module, not from Unité.

q: A retaining wall prevents soil erosion and a pergola provides shade. Under which functional purpose of hardscape do both fall?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Hardscape — Functional Purposes
n: Structural support is the purpose covering retaining walls that prevent soil erosion and pergolas that provide shade. Accessibility and flow is the near miss, but that heading covers paths, stairs, and ramps guiding movement, while visual anchor covers hardscape acting as a focal point.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: For courtyards and patios, which trees are recommended, with which examples?
o: Columnar trees such as Italian Cypress
Broad canopy or umbrella trees such as Rain Trees or Acacias
Pyramidal trees such as Pine or Spruce
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Using Trees as Shade Elements — Courtyards and patios
n: Courtyards and patios call for broad canopy or umbrella trees such as Rain Trees or Acacias, because those spaces need coverage over an area people occupy. Columnar trees give almost no overhead cover and are recommended for lining walkways instead.

q: Paimio Sanatorium was designed around the needs of which patients, addressing which three conditions?
o: Tuberculosis patients; sunlight, ventilation, and hygiene
Surgical patients; sterility, anaesthesia, and recovery time
Psychiatric patients; quiet, security, and supervision
Elderly residents; mobility, handrails, and level access
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Paimio Sanatorium, Impact
n: The building was designed around the needs of tuberculosis patients, for whom sunlight, ventilation, and hygiene were the treatment itself before antibiotics existed. This is what makes the design human-centered and its aesthetics functional rather than decorative.

q: Which elements of a landscape make up the hardscape?
o: The below-grade drainage and utilities only
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Hardscape
n: Hardscape is made of the non-living, solid, man-made elements of the landscape; it gives structure, stability, and function to outdoor areas and forms the framework within which softscape is arranged. The living components are softscape, which is the distinction the whole section turns on.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: In tropical climates, which trees are recommended to manage year-round heat and UV exposure?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Using Trees as Shade Elements — Tropical climates
n: Tropical climates call for dense evergreen trees because the heat and UV load never lets up, so the shading must not either. A deciduous tree's leafless period would leave the site exposed exactly when it still needs cover.

q: The Seagram Building was set back from the street, leaving a large open space in front. What did that space become?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Seagram Building
n: The setback space was intended for pedestrians and became an urban plaza that soon turned into a common feature of most New York City skyscrapers. Its point is that it is public and open, which is what a private tenants' garden would not be.

q: Which retaining wall material is described as organic and blending into hilly landscapes?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Retaining Walls, Materials
n: Natural stone is organic and blends into hilly landscapes, so it disappears into a slope rather than announcing itself. Gabion walls use stone too, but the visible cage makes them read as industrial instead.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Within shading terms, the difference between a tall tree and a wide tree is:
o: Taller trees offer overhead shade; wider trees provide lateral coverage
Taller trees offer lateral coverage; wider trees offer overhead shade
Height affects only wind, not shade
Both provide identical shade if canopy density matches
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: How Trees Provide Effective Sun Shading — Height and Branch Spread
n: Taller trees offer overhead shade, while wide trees provide lateral coverage — the shadow reaches sideways rather than straight down. That distinction is what decides whether a tree shades a roof or a wall.

q: What did the Farnsworth House popularize?
o: Prefabricated panels, kit-of-parts assembly, and DIY housing
Rooftop gardens, communal corridors, and modular flats
Colour-coded services, flexible halls, and exposed ducts
Glass houses, open interiors, and minimalism
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House, Modern Influence
n: The house popularized glass houses, open interiors, and minimalism. Rooftop gardens and communal corridors belong to Unité d'Habitation, and the kit-of-parts idea to the Case Study Houses.

q: Which driveway surface allows water to seep through, supporting sustainability?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Driveways and Parking Areas, Examples
n: Permeable pavers allow water to seep through, which supports sustainability by letting rainfall reach the ground rather than running off. This is the same logic the module later credits with managing stormwater and preventing flooding.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: What kind of shade do palms provide, and how should they therefore be used?
o: "Dappled" or minimal shade; for aesthetic framing rather than passive cooling of large facades
Seasonal shade; for winter solar access
Dense overhead shade; as the primary passive cooling strategy for large facades
Low-level shade; as a windbreak along boundaries
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Palm Trees, Effectiveness in Sun shading
n: Unlike deciduous trees, palms give "dappled" or minimal shade, so they belong in an aesthetic framing role rather than as the main passive cooling strategy for a large facade. Treating a row of palms as a cooling device is the mistake this passage exists to prevent.

q: Which set of five items makes up the "Five Points of Architecture" manifested by Villa Savoye?
o: Pilotis, pitched roof, cellular plan, vertical windows, load-bearing façade
Pilotis, flat roof terrace, open plan, horizontal windows, free façade
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye, Impact
n: The five points are pilotis, the flat roof terrace, the open plan, horizontal windows, and the free façade — each a consequence of moving structure off the wall and onto columns. The list of symmetry, hierarchy, rhythm, proportion, and scale belongs to the design principles section of this module, not to Le Corbusier's manifesto.

q: Which water feature is described as either cascading over rocks or built into a wall, and as adding sound movement?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Water Features, Examples
n: Waterfalls either cascade over rocks or are built into a wall, and they add sound movement to a landscape. Fountains are the other moving-water option, but they are described by their range of styles from tiered classical to modern minimal jets.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which tree shape has downward drooping branches, gives diffused shade, and is best placed near water features and meditative spaces?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The weeping shape, illustrated by the Weeping Willow, has downward drooping branches and gives diffused shade with a dramatic, soft ambiance suited to water features and meditative spaces. Its selection is driven by mood as much as by shading.

q: The number of storeys does the Seagram Building have, and what does it stand on is:
o: 58 storeys on a steel truss podium
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Seagram Building
n: The reviewer gives it as a 38-storey office building set on bronze-clad pillars, which was avant-garde for its time. The bronze cladding is the detail worth holding — it is what gives the tower its dark, precise character.

q: Which landscape principle avoids clutter by keeping the design clean and intentional?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Simplicity
n: Simplicity avoids clutter by keeping the design clean and intentional. Variety is its natural opponent, introducing difference — a landscape needs both, kept in check against each other.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Why have many palm species evolved to survive high-wind events such as typhoons?
o: Because their root balls anchor deeper than other trees
Because their trunks are unusually rigid and resist bending
Because of their flexible trunks and aerodynamic fronds
Because they shed all their fronds at the first gust
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Palm Trees
n: Palms survive typhoons through flexible trunks and aerodynamic fronds — they bend and let the wind pass rather than resisting it. Rigidity is the opposite strategy and is what causes brittle trees to snap.

q: The Bauhaus School building is located in Germany. What period does the reviewer give for it?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Bauhaus School
n: The entry dates the Bauhaus School to 1925–1933. The 1919 date is the plausible distractor because that is when the school itself was founded, but the building in this list is the later Dessau period.

q: In landscape balance, which pairing is correct?
o: Both symmetrical and asymmetrical are formal
Symmetrical is formal; asymmetrical is informal but still visually stable
Symmetrical is informal; asymmetrical is formal
Symmetrical is stable; asymmetrical is inherently unstable
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Balance
n: Symmetrical balance is formal, while asymmetrical balance is informal but still visually stable. The word "still" carries the point: informality does not mean the composition tips over.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Palm trees are monocots. What does that classification mean about their seeds?
o: The seeds contain two embryonic leaves and a taproot
The seeds contain only one embryonic leaf, or cotyledon
The seeds germinate only after fire
The seeds are enclosed in a cone rather than a fruit
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Palm Trees
n: Monocots are flowering plants whose seeds contain only one embryonic leaf, the cotyledon — the botanical fact behind the palm's single unbranched stem and crown of fronds. Cone-borne seeds are the mark of conifers, an entirely different group.

q: The Bauhaus is said to have influenced everything from IKEA furniture to what other two things?
o: Theme park design and immersive storytelling
Gothic revival churches and cathedral restoration
Modular housing and modern design education
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Bauhaus School, Modern Influence
n: Its influence runs from IKEA furniture to modular housing to modern design education — the last being the curriculum model most design schools still follow. Theme park design belongs to a different section of this module entirely.

q: Which landscape principle uses differences in colour, texture, and shape to add interest?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Contrast and Variety
n: Contrast and variety use differences in colour, texture, and shape to add interest to a landscape. Unity works the other way, seeking consistency — the two principles are meant to be held in tension.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: A narrow trunk with a widening canopy, illustrated by Crape Myrtle, describes which shape?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The vase-shaped tree has a narrow trunk with a widening canopy, gives moderate shade, and works for layered plantings in small gardens and along streets. The narrow base is what lets it sit beside a path without obstructing it.

q: The Salk Institute of 1965 is located where?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Salk Institute
n: The Salk Institute was built in California in 1965. Pennsylvania is the plausible distractor because Louis Kahn practised in Philadelphia, but the institute itself overlooks the Pacific.

q: Which set of characteristics belongs to gardens rather than parks?
o: Free, publicly funded, and designed to promote social equity
Artistic and botanical, thematically arranged, and personal, intimate, and contemplative
Inclusive, community oriented, and multi-zoned for sports and concerts
Protected, minimally interfered with, and managed for conservation
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Garden — Key Characteristics
n: Gardens are artistic and botanical in nature, carefully arranged with themes such as colour, plant species, and symmetry, and are more personal, intimate, and contemplative — sometimes also serving scientific or educational purposes. Being inclusive, multi-zoned, and free is what characterises a park.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which species are singled out as providing some of the thickest, most effective thermal buffers against tropical heat?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Fruit-bearing, Effectiveness in Sun shading
n: Mango and Star Apple, or Caimito, provide some of the thickest and most effective thermal buffers against tropical heat. Their canopies are dense enough that the shade benefit rivals the fruit benefit.

q: The "Bilbao Effect" is:
o: The rise in construction costs when digital fabrication is used
The tendency of titanium to weather unevenly in coastal air
The idea that a single iconic building can revitalize a city's economy
The distortion of scale caused by curved façades
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, Impact
n: The "Bilbao Effect" is the idea that one iconic building can revitalize a city's economy, and the same project moved architecture into the era of BIM, or Building Information Modeling. The term is about urban economics, not about the material's behaviour.

q: In a Japanese Zen garden, what do raked sand and carefully placed rocks represent?
o: Raked sand represents fields; rocks represent villages
Raked sand represents clouds; rocks represent islands
Raked sand represents water; rocks represent mountains
Raked sand represents wind; rocks represent trees
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Japanese Zen Gardens
n: Zen gardens use dry elements symbolically: raked sand stands for water and carefully placed rocks for mountains, all in service of meditation, reflection, and Zen Buddhism. The symbolism is what allows a landscape with no water to be read as one.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Because many fruit trees have aggressive, thirsty root systems that can crack foundations or sidewalks, where should they be kept?
o: Directly beside driveways where the paving is thickest
In raised planters within pedestrian plazas
In "soft" areas such as lawns or gardens, away from high-traffic paths and parking slots
Along building edges where roots are confined
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Fruit-bearing Trees
n: Fruit trees are best kept in "soft" areas such as lawns or gardens, away from high-traffic pedestrian paths and parking slots, so their roots have somewhere to go and their fruit falls harmlessly. Planting them beside paving invites both the cracking and the staining problem at once.

q: Which publication sponsored the Case Study Houses programme, and what was the programme trying to answer?
o: Arts & Architecture magazine; the postwar building boom
Architectural Record; the shortage of civic buildings
Domus; the revival of European craft
The Architectural Review; the decline of the country house
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Case Study Houses
n: Arts & Architecture magazine sponsored the programme, which sought to respond to the postwar building boom with prototype modern homes that were easily replicated and affordable to the average American. Affordability and replicability are the two conditions that made it an experiment rather than a set of custom villas.

q: Which World Heritage site, with an orchid garden and rainforest trail, is given as the example of a botanical garden?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Botanical Gardens, Example
n: The Singapore Botanic Gardens is the botanical garden example — a World Heritage site with an orchid garden and rainforest trail. Baguio Botanical Garden is the near miss because of its name, but the module lists it under tropical gardens.

q: Landscaping can define zones such as patios, courtyards, and play areas. What are these called?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Functional Extension of Space
n: These defined zones are called outdoor rooms, and they extend living or working spaces outdoors. The term is deliberate — the landscape is being treated as architecture rather than as surrounding ground.

q: What kind of later buildings did the Salk Institute inspire?
o: Commercial towers with plazas and clean grids
Prefabricated homes with open plans and industrial materials
Institutional buildings with meditative spaces, minimalism, and environmental integration
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Salk Institute, Modern Influence
n: It inspired institutional buildings with meditative spaces, minimalism, and environmental integration — the contemplative courtyard being its most copied idea. Commercial towers with plazas trace back to the Seagram Building instead.

q: Which garden type is designed to look natural but is in fact highly planned, using winding paths, irregular clumps of trees, and hidden vistas?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Informal Gardens
n: Informal gardens are designed to look natural while being highly planned, using winding paths, irregular clumps of trees, and hidden vistas to mimic the romanticized countryside and encourage exploration and a sense of discovery. The word "planned" is what separates this from genuine wilderness.

q: Landscaping supports biodiversity by attracting which creatures, and what does that foster?
o: Rodents and reptiles; a natural pest cycle
Fish and amphibians; a wetland habitat
Livestock and poultry; a productive landscape
Birds, butterflies, and beneficial insects; an ecological balance
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Environmental Benefits
n: Landscaping attracts birds, butterflies, and beneficial insects, fostering an ecological balance. Rodents appear elsewhere in this module, but as a nuisance drawn by unharvested fruit rather than as a biodiversity benefit.

q: The Seagram Building is described as the foundation for which later building types?
o: Modern corporate buildings and urban skyscrapers
Suburban tract housing and strip malls
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Seagram Building, Modern Influence
n: It is named the foundation for most modern corporate buildings and urban skyscrapers, and it determined the look and scope of New York architecture from the late 1950s onward. Suburban housing prototypes belong instead to the Case Study Houses.

q: Scientific plant labeling, arboretums, and thematic zones are the design elements of which garden type?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Botanical Gardens
n: Botanical gardens exist for plant conservation, education, and display, and use scientific plant labeling, arboretums, and thematic zones. The labeling is the tell — it signals that the garden's purpose is educational rather than purely aesthetic.

q: Which three devices are named as blurring the line between indoors and outdoors?
o: Terraces, green walls, and large windows opening to gardens
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Effects of Landscaping — Integration and Sustainability in Design
n: Terraces, green walls, and large windows opening to gardens are what blur the line between indoors and outdoors. Each connects the interior to planting specifically, which is what distinguishes them from devices that merely admit daylight.

q: The Seagram Building was completed in 1958 in which city?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Seagram Building
n: The Seagram Building stands on Park Avenue in New York and dates to 1958. Chicago is the plausible miss because Mies van der Rohe practised there for decades, but the tower that reset New York's skyline is the Seagram.

q: National parks are large tracts of land protected by the government. What is their stated function?
o: To provide free recreation space in dense cities
To protect natural heritage and biodiversity
To conserve historic buildings and monuments
To generate revenue through commercial recreation
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — National Parks
n: National parks function to protect natural heritage and biodiversity, covering land in its natural, semi-natural, or developed state. Commercial recreation revenue is the theme park's function, which is the sharpest contrast in this list.

q: Under aesthetic enhancement, what does it mean that landscaping "creates visual harmony"?
o: It repeats the same species throughout the site
It matches the colour of the paving to the roof
It complements the architectural style, whether modern, tropical, minimalist, or classical
It hides the building behind dense planting
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping in Architecture — Aesthetic Enhancement
n: Creating visual harmony means the landscape complements the architectural style — modern, tropical, minimalist, or classical. The landscape is being tuned to the building, not used to conceal it.

q: Toward which direction did the Guggenheim Bilbao move architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, Modern Influence
n: Its modern influence was to move architecture toward deconstructivist form-finding — shapes discovered through modelling rather than derived from a rational grid. Rationalist standardisation describes the modernist position the building broke from.

q: Which statement belongs to the cultural and social impact of parks?
o: They restrict access to protect fragile habitats
They serve as a buffer against urban stress and are accessible to all regardless of economic class
They generate rental income for adjacent landowners
They are reserved for organised sporting use
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Park — Cultural and Social Impact
n: Parks encourage socialization and healthy lifestyles, host cultural and community events, serve as a buffer against urban stress, and are accessible to all regardless of economic class. Restricted access describes national parks' conservation approach, not the general social role of parks.

q: Under environmental benefits, how does landscaping improve air quality?
o: Plants convert carbon dioxide into mulch
Plants block wind and prevent pollutant dispersal
Plants absorb pollutants and release oxygen
Plants raise humidity and trap dust permanently
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Environmental Benefits
n: Landscaping improves air quality because plants absorb pollutants and release oxygen. Blocking wind would in fact hinder dispersal, so it is the opposite of an air-quality benefit.

q: The Farnsworth House is characterised as an elevated box made entirely of glass and steel with no interior walls. What two qualities does that emphasise?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House, Impact
n: Removing the interior walls and glazing the envelope emphasises transparency and connection to nature — the surrounding landscape becomes the wall. Privacy is what such a house conspicuously sacrifices, which is why it remains controversial as a dwelling.

q: Which Philippine UNESCO site, known for biodiversity and sustainable tourism, is the national park example?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — National Parks, Example
n: The Palawan Underground River Park is the national park example — a UNESCO site known for biodiversity and sustainable tourism. Baguio Botanical Garden is also Philippine but appears in this module as the tropical garden example.

q: What does landscaping do when it "softens hard edges"?
o: It lowers the surface temperature of paving
It reduces the acoustic reflectivity of glass
Organic elements contrast with and balance sharp building lines and materials like concrete or glass
It rounds off the corners of the building's massing
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping in Architecture — Aesthetic Enhancement
n: Softening hard edges means organic elements contrast with and balance the sharp lines and hard materials — concrete or glass — of the building. It is a visual effect achieved by juxtaposition, not a physical alteration of the building.

q: Paimio Sanatorium integrated furniture, lighting, and colour psychology into healing environments. What is it therefore called the basis for?
o: Corporate office planning, open-plan workspaces, and hot-desking
Deconstructivist museums, sculptural form, and digital modelling
High-Tech architecture, exposed services, and flexible halls
Contemporary hospital design, therapeutic architecture, and biophilic design
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Paimio Sanatorium, Modern Influence
n: By treating furniture, lighting, and colour as part of the therapy, Paimio became the basis for contemporary hospital design, therapeutic architecture, and biophilic design. Its concern is the patient's experience, which is what separates it from the technological interests of High-Tech architecture.

q: Which set gives the design considerations for national parks?
o: Efficient use of limited space and low-maintenance plants
Minimal human interference, eco-tourism, and conservation
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — National Parks, Design Considerations
n: National park design considerations are minimal human interference, eco-tourism, and conservation. Minimal interference is the operative principle — the design goal is to build as little as possible.

q: An observer can tell what a building is for, where it came from, or what its designer intended just by looking at it. Which quality is that?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Architectural Character (Pevsner, N., 1943, An Outline of European Architecture)
n: Character refers to the expressive qualities that let an observer identify a building's purpose, origin, or the intent of the designer — the quality that makes a building look like what it is meant to be. Hierarchy also concerns legibility, but only of importance within one composition.

q: Which three later tendencies did Maison de Verre influence?
o: Rooftop gardens, communal corridors, and modular flats
Mixed-use buildings, industrial interior aesthetics, and transparency in design
Eco-tourism, conservation, and minimal human interference
Symmetry, natural light, and raw concrete
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Maison de Verre, Modern Influence
n: Its modern influence is on mixed-use buildings, industrial interior aesthetics, and transparency in design — each traceable to the house's dual programme and its glass-block wall. Raw concrete and symmetry describe the Salk Institute instead.

q: Which is given as the example of a theme park?
o: The Magic Kingdom at Walt Disney World Resort, Florida
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Theme Parks, Example
n: The Magic Kingdom at Walt Disney World Resort in Florida is the theme park example. It illustrates all three of the type's design considerations — ride safety, fantasy architecture, and immersive storytelling — in one place.

q: A courthouse looks like a courthouse because its appearance derives from what happens inside it. Which type of character is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Architectural Character — Functional Character
n: Functional Character is the appearance of a building derived from its internal use. Associated Character is the near miss — that would be a courthouse reading as authoritative because of the cultural memory attached to classical porticoes, rather than because of the courtrooms behind them.

q: Natural or artificial lighting is used in a landscape for which two stated purposes?
o: To reduce heat gain and shade paving
To accelerate plant growth and extend flowering
To mask noise and improve privacy
To highlight features and ensure safety
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Light
n: Light, natural or artificial, is used to highlight features and to ensure safety — an aesthetic purpose and a practical one together. Masking noise is the job of sound and of dense planting, listed separately.

q: Under "seasonality and change," how are softscapes said to evolve with time?
o: By remaining unchanged if correctly specified
By fading, staining, and requiring resealing
By blooming, shedding leaves, growing fuller, or thinning out
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Softscape — Seasonality and change
n: Softscapes evolve by blooming, shedding leaves, growing fuller, or thinning out. Cracking, settling, and weathering describe how hardscape ages, which is decline rather than growth.

q: Two dissimilar materials are set side by side so that the qualities of each become clearer by comparison with its neighbour. Which term names this state of being placed close together?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Contrast, Juxtaposition
n: Juxtaposition is the state of being placed close together or side-by-side, especially for comparison or contrast, and in architecture it highlights the unique qualities of individual elements by showing how they differ from their neighbors. Contrast is the broader principle; juxtaposition is the specific act of placement that delivers it.
